questions.q: Why do designers establish and review 'criteria to evaluate success' when designing?
options: To increase the number of sales of a product
To ensure environmental factors are considered
To ensure the final design meets the specified needs
To maintain product awareness for further refinement of innovative products
questions.explanation: Criteria to evaluate success are measurable benchmarks drawn from the brief, used to check the final design meets the specified needs. As the episode puts it, the proposal's criteria are 'the factors made specific' — testable targets the design is developed and evaluated against. The other options are narrower commercial or environmental concerns.

questions.q: In the project proposal mnemonic NICe, what are the three parts the proposal must contain?
options: The need, the investors and the cost
The identification and exploration of the need, the areas of investigation, and the measurable criteria to evaluate success
The novelty, the innovation and the concept
The narrative, the illustration and the conclusion
questions.explanation: NICe stands for the Need, the areas of Investigation, and the measurable Criteria to evaluate success. The episode calls these two — NICe and the four-part justify pattern — the spine of the whole module.

questions.q: What is the four-part 'justify, don't narrate' pattern the episode threads through every folio page and Section II answer?
options: Decision, reason, factor, evidence
Define, research, ideate, produce
Need, investigation, criteria, evaluation
Describe, illustrate, explain, conclude
questions.explanation: Justifying (not narrating) means stating the decision, giving the reason, naming the factor affecting design, and pointing to the evidence — decision, reason, factor, evidence. This pattern earns the higher bands because it shows a reasoned, evidence-based process rather than just describing what was done.

questions.q: Using a variety of research methods in the process of design is important because it
options: helps develop marketing strategies.
improves understanding of customer needs.
promotes the use of emerging technologies.
protects the intellectual property of the designer.
questions.explanation: Using varied research methods triangulates data from different sources, giving the designer a fuller, more reliable understanding of customer needs. This is the QISOTS research stage the episode applies — research and experimentation produce the evidence that justifies decisions. The other options are not the central reason for researching.

questions.q: The episode re-flags the headline HSC trap. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two lists?
options: FFA EQ NEW LOAd are the eleven factors affecting design (H1.1); TEMPLE are the six factors affecting the success of an innovation (H3.1)
FFA EQ NEW LOAd are the six factors affecting innovation; TEMPLE are the eleven factors affecting design
Both lists describe the same eleven factors using different mnemonics
FFA EQ NEW LOAd are research methods; TEMPLE are the stages of the design process
questions.explanation: Don't confuse the eleven factors affecting design (FFA EQ NEW LOAd, outcome H1.1), which you apply and use to analyse success and failure, with the six factors affecting the success of an innovation (TEMPLE, outcome H3.1) met in module H2. Different lists, different outcomes, often both in one paper.

questions.q: Successful completion of a major design project depends on a student making the correct link between
options: action and time management.
sustainability and appropriateness of materials.
experimentation and development of practical skills.
generation of concept designs and organising materials.
questions.explanation: Completing a major project relies on linking the action plan to the time plan so tasks are sequenced and scheduled realistically. The other pairings are useful but do not directly determine whether the whole project is finished.

questions.q: From memory: what are the five stages of the front-half MDP arc, and which DRIPER stages do they run as?
keyPoints: Orient to the task and adopt the justify-not-narrate habit.
Write the NICe project proposal (need, areas of investigation, measurable criteria).
Apply the eleven factors (FFA EQ NEW LOAd) and analyse success and failure through them.
Study designers and emulate their process, then research and experiment, responding to the findings.
Together this early development runs as DRIPER's Define, Research and Ideate stages.
questions.explanation: If you recalled orient, propose, analyse-with-factors, learn-from-designers, research — and linked it to DRIPER's Define/Research/Ideate — grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Name the four mnemonics carrying the front half of the module, and the one habit that threads through everything.
keyPoints: DRIPER — the design process the MDP runs on.
NICe — the proposal: need, areas of investigation, criteria.
FFA EQ NEW LOAd — the eleven factors affecting design.
QISOTS — the research methods (from module three) applied now.
The through-line habit: justify, don't narrate — decision, reason, factor, evidence.
questions.explanation: Four hooks plus one habit. If you got all four mnemonics and the decision-reason-factor-evidence pattern, mark it Easy; if you missed QISOTS or the pattern, mark it Hard or Again.

questions.q: Outline how testing and experimenting can improve a design project.
questions.modelAnswer: Testing and experimenting improve a design project by letting the designer explore the successes and failures of different materials, tools and techniques before committing to them. This saves time, money and material wastage and leads to a better-resolved final design.

criteria.descriptor: Outlines relevant information regarding testing and experimenting and how it can improve a design

questions.explanation: This is the research-and-experiment stage of early development: experiments generate and test ideas, and the findings are responded to by refining the design — for example selecting the strongest joint after testing. The verb 'respond' is where the mark is.

questions.q:
Research is important in the early stages of designing a new product.

Explain the factors a designer would need to consider when interpreting and applying research data.
questions.modelAnswer: When interpreting and applying research data the designer must consider how relevant, reliable and current the data is, and how directly it relates to the identified need and the project's criteria. Reliable, relevant findings are then responded to by modifying decisions — selecting a stronger material or adjusting a dimension — so the design is built on evidence rather than assumption, and the documented findings become the justification for those decisions.

criteria.descriptor: Makes the relationship between the factors and the consideration evident (when interpreting and applying research data); provides the reasons why the designer considers these factors
Provides characteristics and features of the factors a designer would need to consider when interpreting and applying research data
Sketches in general terms factors a designer would consider when interpreting and applying research data
Identifies a factor a designer would consider when interpreting and applying research data

questions.explanation: Research only adds value when it actually changes decisions — the evaluate-and-refine loop. The designer must weigh the relevance and reliability of data against the need and criteria, then respond to it, which also produces the evidence that justifies folio decisions.
